title: Generic Powered Parachute — Emergency Procedures (FAA Powered Parachute Flying Handbook)
description: Emergency procedures for certificated powered parachutes (PPC), transcribed from the FAA Powered Parachute Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-12A), Chapter 12, a US Government work in the public domain. Covers engine failure on climbout, engine failure in flight, water landing, in-flight fire, takeoff abort, wing anomalies (wall, lock-out, line-over, rollover), and porpoising. IMPORTANT: The Handbook explicitly states these guidelines are generic and do not replace the manufacturer's recommended procedures. The manufacturer's POH takes precedence wherever there is a conflict.

source.title: Powered Parachute Flying Handbook
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Aviation Administration, Flight Standards Service
source.notes: The Handbook presents emergency procedures as prose paragraphs. Converting to challenge/response format is an editorial act by the transcriber. Numbered steps in the source (e.g., the water landing sequence) are preserved in order. The Handbook's own caution: these guidelines are generic and the manufacturer's POH takes precedence.

known_issues.description: These procedures are generic. No item has been checked against any specific aircraft's POH. The manufacturer's procedures take precedence.
The Handbook covers single-engine PPCs. Twin-engine PPC engine-failure procedures differ significantly — a twin can continue flight on one engine under most conditions.
Specific numeric limits (minimum restart altitude, glide ratios, fuel thresholds) are not provided — they are aircraft-specific and must come from the POH.

sections.title: Engine Failure on Climbout
sections.condition: Engine fails or loses power immediately after liftoff or during initial climb before a safe maneuvering altitude is reached

items.text: Do not attempt to turn back to the field from low altitude. It is safer to establish the proper glide attitude and land straight ahead or slightly to either side of the takeoff path.
Glide attitude
items.detail: When the engine fails at low altitude, the cart swings back under the wing and the wing can surge forward into a dangerous dive. If the wing surges forward, immediately flare to slow the surge; gradually release the flare when the wing is back overhead in normal flying position.

items.text: Landing area
Full flare: approximately 1 second above ground — push both steering bars fully forward
items.response: SMOOTH FULL FLARE — HOLD THROUGH TOUCHDOWN

items.text: After touchdown: collapse canopy immediately

sections.title: Engine Failure In Flight
sections.condition: Engine stops or loses power in flight at altitude

items.text: A powered parachute glides. Loss of engine power is not an immediate catastrophe. Fly the aircraft. Select the safest landing area and glide to it.
Continue to fly the aircraft — maintain wing overhead in normal glide
Landing zone: safest available terrain — into wind if possible
items.detail: Safe terrain is the primary priority; wind direction is secondary. Land into the wind if possible; downwind otherwise. Crosswind is the least favorable. Never fly over terrain you cannot land on given your altitude and glide slope.

items.text: Engine restart: attempt only if altitude and cause permit — do not restart below manufacturer's minimum altitude
items.response: ATTEMPTED IF ALTITUDE PERMITS — OTHERWISE GLIDE TO LANDING

items.text: Full flare approximately 1 second above ground — push both steering bars completely forward and hold
items.response: SMOOTH FULL FLARE — HOLD THROUGH TOUCHDOWN

items.text: After touchdown: collapse canopy (engine already off)

sections.title: Engine Failure In Flight — Water Landing (PPCL)
sections.condition: Engine failure over water with insufficient altitude to glide to shore

items.text: When planning any over-water flight, wear a life vest. Maintain altitude that permits gliding to land at all times. Carry a line-cutter that is accessible but cannot cause injury on impact.
Align into wind and move toward shore if possible
items.response: HEADING INTO WIND, CLOSEST TO SHORE

items.text: Stay seated — cart provides impact protection
All electronics
Objects that may delay evacuation (camera straps, communication cords)
Objects that may penetrate skin on impact
Seatbelt and shoulder harness
At approximately 2 seconds (~25 ft) above water: head, neck, and legs tucked close to body; arms along head with hands over lower back of head
After impact: release seatbelt and shoulder harness and exit cart
If entangled with canopy lines: use line-cutter and work to edge of wing
Swim to shore — do not attempt to retrieve items from aircraft

sections.title: In-Flight Fire
sections.condition: Any sign of fire near the engine, fuel containers, or fuel lines

items.text: In-flight fire is one of the most serious emergencies a PPC pilot can encounter due to the flammability of the ram-air wing. Land immediately.
Throttle
Fuel valve(s)
Magnetos
All electronics
Land immediately — stop as quickly as possible
Evacuate the aircraft immediately and move away
items.detail: After evacuating, the principal danger is fuel igniting and exploding. Get far away from the aircraft.

sections.title: Rejected Takeoff / Abort
sections.condition: Any condition requiring termination of the takeoff during the ground roll or initial kiting

items.text: Abort conditions include: lines restricted around airframe, wing wall, wing lock-out, line-over detected during rolling preflight, lines caught under a wheel, unsafe wing position.
Throttle
Magneto switches
Maintain directional control: steer clear of obstacles during deceleration
Collapse and pull down canopy
Identify and correct the cause before the next takeoff attempt

sections.title: Line-Over Detected (Ground — Before Takeoff)
sections.condition: A suspension line is observed over the top surface of the wing during preflight or rolling preflight

items.text: A line-over will prevent proper wing inflation and will cause a severe yaw or roll on takeoff. This is a no-go condition. Do not launch.
Abort takeoff: throttle idle, magnetos off
Identify which line is over the wing and which riser group it belongs to
Pull the wing fabric through the loop made by the line-over
Re-inspect all lines before next takeoff attempt

sections.title: Wing Pull-Over (Rollover)
sections.condition: Cart begins to tip over due to horizontal lift from wing not centered over cart

items.text: A rollover can cause death or serious injury. Prevention is by keeping the cart headed into the wind, allowing the wing time to center, and not rushing the takeoff roll.
If cart is lifting on one side but recovery is still possible: immediately reduce engine RPM to reduce wing lift — this may allow the cart to settle back on all wheels.
If past recovery point — magneto switches
Do not try to stop the rollover with arms or legs — pull all limbs into tuck position
After cart stops: unstrap immediately and exit
If safe and not conflicting with 49 CFR 830 accident-reporting requirements, return the cart to upright position to prevent fuel and oil from spilling.

sections.title: Porpoising on Landing Approach
sections.condition: Pilot-induced pitch oscillations developing during approach or landing

items.text: Porpoising is caused by rapid or over-controlled throttle movements. There is an inherent delay between throttle change and pitch response. If oscillations begin developing on approach, go around immediately.
Go around: apply full power and climb back to pattern altitude
On next approach: slow, smooth throttle action — avoid over-control

sections.title: Wing Wall on Takeoff Roll
sections.condition: The canopy forms a wall-shape behind the cart: trailing edge on ground, leading edge vertical, wing not inflating and rising

items.text: The only safe solution to a wing wall is to abort, shut down, and re-lay the canopy. Attempting to 'pop' the wing out of the wall with throttle movements risks sucking lines into the propeller.
Abort the takeoff: throttle idle, magnetos off
Re-lay canopy from the beginning

sections.title: Wing Lock-Out on Takeoff Roll
sections.condition: The inflated canopy hangs at approximately 45 degrees behind the cart and will not rise overhead despite increasing groundspeed

items.text: Two techniques exist to recover from a lock-out on a rectangular wing. Consult your flight instructor before attempting these on an elliptical wing, as the characteristics differ significantly.
Method 1 — Reduce groundspeed until wing begins to fall back and down; then smoothly and firmly increase groundspeed to slingshot wing overhead before it touches the ground
items.response: WING OVERHEAD — LOC CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

items.text: Method 2 — Maintain groundspeed and apply full flare (push both steering bars); hold until wing pulls back to approximately 60 degrees; then smoothly release flare to slingshot wing overhead
items.response: WING OVERHEAD — LOC CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

items.text: If neither technique brings the wing overhead cleanly, abort the takeoff. Do not launch with a lock-out.
